questions.problem: Find a parametric equation of the plane that passes through the point $S(1,-3,4)$ and is parallel to the vectors ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$  and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
A parametric equation of a plane is given by 

$$
r=p+sb+tc,
$$

where $p$ is the position vector of a point on the plane and the vectors $b$ and $c$ are parallel to the plane but not to each other.

Here, the position vector of the given point $S$ is $p=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]$, and the two vectors that are parallel to the plane (but not to each other) are ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$  and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

So, a parametric equation of the plane is given by

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+s[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,s,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

questions.problem:
Find a normal vector to the plane

$$
r=⟨2,0,-1⟩+t⟨-2,-7,5⟩+s⟨2,12,5⟩,\,t,\,s\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
From the parametric equation, we have that $v=⟨-2,-7,5⟩$ and $w=⟨2,12,5⟩$ are parallel to the plane.

Now, we need to find a normal vector of the plane. To do that, we use the cross product of $v$ and $w$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =v\times w \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -7 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\times [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 12 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -2 & -7 & 5 \\ 2 & 12 & 5\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-95i+20j-10k \\  & =⟨-95,20,-10⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨-95,20,-10⟩.$

Find a normal vector to the plane 

$$
\mathbf{r}= \langle -6,3, 2 \rangle + t \langle 4, 2, -1 \rangle + s \langle 4, -3, 2 \rangle,\qquad t,\,s \in (-\infty,\infty).
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the parametric equation, we have that $\mathbf{v} = \langle 4, 2, -1 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{w} = \langle 4, -3, 2 \rangle$ are parallel to the plane.

Now, we need to find a normal vector of the plane. To do that, we use the cross product of $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{w}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =v\times w \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\times [\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 4 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =i-12j-20k \\  & =⟨1,-12,-20⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}=\langle 1, -12, -20 \rangle.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equation of the Plane Parallel To Two Lines
canonical_examples.problem: Find a parametric equation of the plane that passes through the point $C(2,50,-19)$ and is parallel to the lines $\mathbf{r}= \langle 2,\sqrt{6},17 \rangle + s \langle -1,7,2 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{r}= \langle 20,-44, 27 \rangle + t \langle 2\sqrt{3},9,-8 \rangle$.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The direction vectors of the lines are $\mathbf{v_1}=\langle  -1,7,2  \rangle$ and $\mathbf{v_2}=\langle 2\sqrt{3},9,-8 \rangle$, respectively. These vectors are parallel to the plane but not to each other.

We also know that the point $C(2,50,-19)$ lies on the plane and its position vector is $\mathbf{c}=\langle 2,50,-19 \rangle.$  

So, the corresponding parametric equation of the plane is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =c+s{v}_{1}+t{v}_{2} \\ r & =⟨2,50,-19⟩+s\,⟨-1,7,2⟩+t\,⟨2\sqrt{3},9,-8⟩,\,s,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equation of the Plane Passing Through Three Given Points
canonical_examples.problem: Find a parametric equation of the plane that passes through the points $A(-1,4,-3),$ $B(7,5,4),$ and $C(2,-2,8).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we need to find two vectors that are parallel to the plane (but not to each other). Let's use the displacement vectors $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨7,5,4⟩-⟨-1,4,-3⟩ \\  & =⟨8,1,7⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =⟨2,-2,8⟩-⟨-1,4,-3⟩ \\  & =⟨3,-6,11⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if we consider the position vector $\mathbf{a}=\langle -1,4,-3 \rangle$ of the point $A,$ then the corresponding parametric equation of the plane is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =a+s\overset{\to }{AB}+t\overset{\to }{AC} \\ r & =⟨-1,4,-3⟩+s⟨8,1,7⟩+t⟨3,-6,11⟩,\,s,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

**Watch out!** The form of the final equation depends on our choice of vectors and the point on the plane. We could have picked other vectors. Likewise, we could have chosen $B$ or $C$ instead of $A$ as our point on the plane. So, the answer is *not unique*!
